sourceCopy.name: Square Root Simplifier
sourceCopy.title: Square Root Simplifier Free | UsefulVerse
sourceCopy.description: Simplify square and nth roots exactly, or rationalize a square-root denominator. Free browser calculator with no sign-up.
sourceCopy.intro: Simplify exact integer radicals by extracting perfect powers, or rewrite a fraction so its denominator contains no square root. Results are exact for the supported integer inputs.
sourceCopy.howQuestion: How do you simplify a square root?
sourceCopy.howAnswer: Factor the radicand into prime powers. Pull each complete pair outside a square root; for example, √72 = √(36 × 2) = 6√2. This tool also supports integer roots with indexes 2 through 12.
sourceCopy.privacyAnswer: No. The calculation runs in this browser and this tool does not upload or save your inputs.

fields.rationalizeMode: Remove a square root from a denominator
fields.denominatorCoefficient: Coefficient multiplying the square root in the denominator
fields.rationalizeRadicand: Positive integer under the denominator’s square root
fields.limitsNote: Enter whole numbers. Radicands are limited to ±1,000,000,000,000; the root index is 2–12. Negative radicands are supported only for odd indexes.
fields.rationalizeNote: This mode handles numerator / (coefficient × √radicand). The denominator coefficient cannot be zero; the radicand must be a positive whole number.
fields.rationalized: Equivalent form with a rational denominator
fields.rationalizationExplanation: Multiply the numerator and denominator by the same square root, then reduce the rational coefficient.

messages.checkInputs: Check the whole numbers, root index, and denominator.
messages.copyUnavailable: Copy is not available in this browser.

additionalFaqs.question: Can it rationalize a denominator?
additionalFaqs.answer: Yes. It rewrites a / (c√b) with integer inputs as an equivalent fraction whose denominator has no square root, then reduces the rational coefficient.

additionalFaqs.question: Does this give decimal approximations?
additionalFaqs.answer: No. It keeps the exact radical form. Use a scientific calculator if you also need a decimal approximation.
